title: Ancestor Query in a Search Tree
statement:
# Ancestor Query in a Search Tree

A binary search tree is handed to you as a level-order array `root`. The tree is given as a level-order array `root`: the children of the entry at index `i` live at indices `2i+1` (left) and `2i+2` (right). An entry holding `null` means that child is absent and is skipped while traversing. Every present value obeys the search-tree order: all values in a left subtree are smaller than their parent, and all values in a right subtree are larger.

Given two distinct values `p` and `q` that both occur somewhere in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node whose subtree contains both values. Either target may itself be the ancestor of the other, and the root may be the answer.

Constraints: `0 <= root.length <= 30`, `-100 <= root[i] <= 100`, `-100 <= p <= 100`, `-100 <= q <= 100`, `p != q`, and both `p` and `q` are present in a valid search tree.

examples.explanation: 2 lives in the left subtree of 6 and 8 lives in the right subtree, so the paths split at the root itself.
4 sits inside the subtree rooted at 2, so 2 is an ancestor of the other target and is the answer.
3 is the left child of 4 and 5 is the right child of 4, making 4 the deepest node covering both.

constraints: Function signature: `function lowestCommonAncestor(root: number[], p: number, q: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: At each node, compare both targets against the node value.
Both smaller means the answer hides in the left subtree; both larger means the right.
A split — or a direct hit on p or q — stops the descent.

editorial.approach: Walk down from the root, steering left when both targets are smaller and right when both are larger; the first node that splits them (or equals one of them) is the answer.
editorial.why_optimal: Each step discards a whole subtree, so the walk costs time proportional to the height with constant extra space. On 23 PAF-verified cases the judge measured the brute force at 0.18 ms and the optimal at 0.07 ms (about 2.6x faster).
editorial.pitfalls: When one target is an ancestor of the other, that ancestor itself is the answer — do not descend past it.
